notes.text: Assamese turned the old s sound into a soft x, like the h in huge. Xaru means small.
Nomoskar is the formal one. Friends skip it entirely and open with kene ase: how are you doing?
Respect lives in the verb here. Tumi koraa for a friend, apuni kore for an elder. The pronoun is only half of it.
Deuta is father, aai is mother, but many Assamese call a beloved daughter aai too. Affection borrows the word.
Khar has no English name. It is an alkaline dish made from burnt banana peel, and every meal traditionally starts with it.
Assamese counts in lakh and kuti, not millions. Ek lakh is a hundred thousand, and every price tag uses it.
Xeuji is green, and it doubles for raw or unripe. A green mango and green grass share one word.
Ask for the ghat, not the port. Assam moves on the Brahmaputra, and ferry crossings still name the towns.
Kali means both yesterday and tomorrow. The verb tense tells you which one, so listen to the ending.
Say kiman daam to ask the price. In a village haat, the first number is always an invitation, not a decision.
Bhal ne means are you well, but people also use it as plain hello. Health and greeting overlap.
A chang ghar stands on stilts above flood water. The word survives even in cities where nobody floods.
Kaam means work and also errand and also usefulness. Kamor manuh is a person who gets things done.
Mon means heart and mind at once. Mon nai does not mean heartless, it means I do not feel like it.
Bihu comes three times a year: spring, autumn, winter. Say Rongali, Kongali or Bhogali so people know which.
